newsitem.title: UK: U.S. heart attack victims survive better - survey.
newsitem.headline: U.S. heart attack victims survive better - survey.

text.p: Victims of a common form of heart attack have a far better chance of survival in the United States than in other developed countries, an international survey of almost 3,000 patients found.
A report on the survey in the British medical journal The Lancet said that while two-thirds of non-U.S. patients suffering cardiogenic shock were dead within 30 days, half the U.S. patients survived.
Cardiogenic shock, which is associated with low blood pressure and poor circulation, accounts for about half the deaths in hospital from heart attacks.
The international trial involved patients in 15 countries but the report did not give details of survival rates in individual countries other than the United States.
"We found small but significant differences in baseline clinical characteristics of patients with cardiogenic shock between those treated in the U.S. and those treated elsewhere," it said.
"However, these differences did not fully account for the significant difference in 30-day mortality."

The doctors reporting the results, which came from the United States, Belgium, the Netherlands and New Zealand, suggested the difference might be because doctors in the United States use certain diagnostic procedures more than other physicians.
Another reason might be that American doctors were more likely to use aggressive therapeutic techniques, including those aimed at re-establishing blood circulation, the survey said.
However, it added: "We cannot say for sure that the difference in survival...was the result of more aggressive treatement strategies."
